extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, legal scholars, judges, policymakers, and biotech industry stakeholders concerned with U.S. §101 patent-eligibility (especially diagnostic/biotech patents)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing whether claimed inventions (particularly diagnostic and biopharmaceutical methods) satisfy U.S. patentable-subject-matter rules under § 101, as interpreted by Supreme Court and Federal Circuit case law. Focuses on tests like the machine-or-transformation rule, categorical exclusions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas), and related doctrines (preemption, mental processes, products of nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical exclusions: laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's excluded categories for patentable subject matter: 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas.' Claims that are drawn to these categories are not patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent in Laboratory Corp. emphasized that such exclusions preserve free access to the 'basic tools' of scientific research. The Court and commentators have struggled to delimit these categories (phenomena of nature, mental processes, abstract concepts). Examples given include e=mc2, the law of gravity, and the heat of the sun. Courts must distinguish claims that preempt these fundamental principles from claims that apply them in a particular, patent-eligible way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed process is surely patent-eligible under § 101 if: (1) it is tied to a particular machine or apparatus, or (2) it transforms a particular article into a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit embraced this as a bright-line rule (e.g., In re Bilski) and applied it extensively to exclude abstract ideas and some diagnostic methods. The Supreme Court described the test as 'a useful and important clue' but not the sole test for process patentability. The test's two prongs have been applied to diverse technologies, and courts have relied on either prong to find eligibility or ineligibility (see Prometheus, Classen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation prong applied to biological/medical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformative steps that change a physical object or the human body (e.g., administering a drug) can satisfy the transformation prong of the machine-or-transformation test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Prometheus the Federal Circuit held that (1) administering a drug transforms the human body, and (2) determining metabolite levels via chemical assays transforms tissue samples — both counted as transformative. Courts assess whether the claimed steps are merely data-gathering or are integral, transformative steps in the treatment or process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine prong: claim tied to a particular machine or apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are tied to a particular machine or apparatus may be patent-eligible under the machine-or-transformation test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilski and subsequent Federal Circuit cases treated machine-implementation as a way to show a claim is not an abstract idea. The absence of a machine-implementation was a reason to invalidate Bilski's hedging method. However, the Supreme Court cautioned that the machine-or-transformation test is not the exclusive test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption / tailored-to-particular-application inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a claim is tailored narrowly enough to encompass only a particular application of a fundamental principle rather than to pre-empt the principle itself; claims that 'entirely preempt' a natural phenomenon or abstract idea are invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Lourie characterized the central issue as whether claims would 'entirely preempt' use of a natural correlation (Gottschalk v. Benson and Parker v. Flook). Prometheus's claims were evaluated for whether they preempted all uses of the recited correlations between metabolite levels and drug efficacy; the panel concluded they did not because they covered particular applications with transformative steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes / 'determine and infer' claims exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that consist primarily of mental processes (determining a fact and inferring a conclusion) can fall within the unpatentable 'mental processes' or 'abstract idea' exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prometheus-type claims often involve: (1) determining a measurable biomarker for an individual and (2) making an inference about health or treatment from that value. Courts assess whether the inference is merely a mental step or whether the claim integrates the determination/inference into a patent-eligible, transformative method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral versus incidental data-gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating transformative steps, courts distinguish between steps that are merely incidental data-gathering and steps that are integral to the claimed application or treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit in Prometheus held that measuring metabolites and administering drugs were integral and not merely incidental, supporting patent eligibility. If a step is only passive data collection, it is less likely to render the claim patent-eligible under transformation-focused analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature / isolated-material chemistry test (covalent bond criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to isolated natural materials (e.g., DNA) may be patent-eligible if isolation requires chemical manipulation such as breaking covalent bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Lourie's opinions looked to chemistry to define product-of-nature boundaries, holding that a claim to isolated DNA can be patentable subject matter if its isolation from its natural environment requires breaking covalent bonds. This is offered as a more concrete, chemistry-based bright-line rule for products of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/judicial approach: bright-line rules vs flexible standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Different courts and judges adopt varying methodologies: the Federal Circuit often prefers bright-line tests for predictability, while the Supreme Court tends to state broad, flexible principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit's preference for clear rules motivated adherence to the machine-or-transformation test; the Supreme Court has criticized rigid approaches and prefers expansive, flexible analyses. This institutional preference shapes how courts formulate and apply eligibility criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimalist (threshold) approach to § 101 exclusions (Judge Rader's view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter exclusions should be treated as a threshold test that does not override the broad statutory categories unless the disqualifying characteristic 'exhibit[s] itself so manifestly' as to override the Patent Act's framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this approach, courts should avoid excluding inventions at the § 101 threshold unless a claim so clearly embodies an abstract idea that it would override statutory eligibility. Inventions with specific applications or technological improvements are less likely to be excluded as abstract under this test (see Research Corp. Techs., Ultramercial, and Judge Rader's views in Classen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy rationale for exclusion: preserving access to basic research tools
rubrics_metrics.description: One justification for excluding laws of nature and basic scientific principles from patentability is to preserve free access to 'basic tools' of scientific research and thereby promote innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent in Laboratory Corp. argued that patents on fundamental scientific principles can impede research by (1) causing researchers to avoid using patented ideas, (2) forcing costly searches of patents, (3) requiring complex licensing arrangements, and (4) raising costs of using the information, sometimes prohibitively so. This policy consideration figures into courts' and amici's arguments about the proper scope of § 101 exclusions.
